purpose: Ground JANUS anti-conformity defenses in established human social-influence research while keeping human psychology distinct from machine mechanisms.

historical_anchor.interpretive_note: These demonstrations concern conformity/suggestibility, not a simple lie detector. Mukhina later described proposing the black/white pyramids and sweet-porridge experiments and reported predominantly conforming reactions in filming.

foundational_research.construct: majority conformity under clear perceptual ground truth
foundational_research.core_design: A naive participant answers after a unanimous majority of confederates gives the same incorrect line-length judgment.
foundational_research.key_lesson: A unanimous wrong majority can shift publicly stated judgments even on simple tasks with an obvious answer.

foundational_research.core_design: Asch-style variations compared face-to-face, anonymous and commitment conditions.
foundational_research.key_lesson: Conformity is not one mechanism: normative pressure can change public behavior, while informational influence can alter beliefs about reality. Anonymous/private judgment reduces some normative pressure but does not eliminate all social influence.
The effect of group size depends on the social-influence process and whether responses are public/private and face-to-face/indirect.
Conformity can serve accuracy, belonging and positive self-concept goals; external influence can be subtle and outside awareness.
Conformity is context-sensitive and remains relevant across face-to-face and digital settings; methodology and group identity matter.

human_risk_factors_relevant_to_machine_d: repeated exposure to the same answer
failure to preserve an independent pre-group judgment
translation_rule_for_IO: Human conformity findings motivate machine tests and defenses, but JANUS must not infer that LLM conformity is driven by human needs for belonging, fear of rejection or subjective social experience without separate mechanistic evidence.
